title: Oracle plans fresh August layoffs as its AI spending spree bites
excerpt: Oracle is planning another round of job cuts this month, even as it pours tens of billions into AI data centres and takes on record debt.
content_html:
Oracle is planning another round of job cuts this month, according to Business Insider, with some teams reportedly facing double-digit-percentage reductions.

Managers have been told to identify the employees affected, and the goal is to trim payroll before 1 September, the start of the company’s fiscal second quarter. Oracle declined to comment.

It is the latest twist in a story we has been tracking for months: a company shedding people while spending furiously on machines.

The pattern speaks directly to what we have called AI’s real bottleneck, which is no longer chips but capital and consent. Oracle, it seems, is testing how much of both it can stretch.

The fresh cuts land on top of a brutal year. In the fiscal year that ended on 31 May 2026, Oracle eliminated roughly 21,000 jobs, a drop of about 13%, taking headcount from around 162,000 to about 141,000.

The company booked $1.8bn in restructuring charges over the period, with as much as $2.1bn expected before the accounting is done.

What makes the cuts jar is the reason Oracle has offered for them. In its own filings, the firm partly attributed the reductions to the “adoption and deployment of AI technologies.”

In other words, the same technology being sold as a growth engine is also, conveniently, the justification for sending thousands of people home.

Follow the money and the logic becomes clearer, if not more comfortable. Oracle’s capital expenditure hit about $55.7bn in FY2026, up from $21.2bn a year earlier, as it raced to build the data centres underpinning its cloud ambitions. That is an extraordinary sum for a company of Oracle’s size to commit in a single year.

Paying for it has meant reaching deep into the debt markets. Oracle ran an operating cash shortfall of roughly $23.7bn, raised about $43bn in debt over the year, with a further $40bn or so expected, and topped up with $5bn in equity.

The build-out, in short, is being financed on borrowed money rather than out of pocket, a structure that leaves the company exposed if the AI demand it is betting on arrives more slowly than promised.

The underlying business is hardly limping. Revenue grew 17%, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, its answer to Amazon and Microsoft, surged 77% as demand for AI computing power kept climbing. On paper, this is a firm winning the very race it is spending so heavily to enter.

Investors are not convinced, though. Oracle’s shares are down about 26% so far this year, a sharp verdict on a strategy that swaps steady profitability for a wager on future AI demand.

The market appears to be asking whether the returns will ever justify the borrowing, and for now it is unimpressed. A quarter wiped off the share price is not the reaction of a market that believes the story.

Strip away the jargon and the arithmetic is stark. Oracle is cutting human costs to help fund the machines, taking on mountains of debt to do it, and watching its own valuation slide while it waits for the bet to pay off. It is a clean illustration of the AI-capex squeeze now running through much of the industry.

Oracle is far from alone in making that trade. Across the sector, firms have been converting payroll into AI capital expenditure, treating salaries as a cost to be redirected toward silicon and server halls. What is unusual about Oracle is how nakedly the numbers lay the choice bare.

For the thousands facing this month’s cuts, the macroeconomic framing offers cold comfort. These are real jobs, in real teams, being removed to hit a deadline set by the calendar and the balance sheet.

Whether the gamble on AI eventually vindicates Oracle’s spending, the people paying for it now will not be around to find out.

content_html_zh:
据 Business Insider 报道，甲骨文计划本月进行另一轮裁员，据报道，一些团队面临两位数的裁员。

经理们被告知要确定受影响的员工，目标是在 9 月 1 日（公司第二财季开始）之前削减工资。 甲骨文拒绝置评。

这是我们几个月来一直在追踪的一个故事的最新转折：一家公司在裁员的同时在机器上疯狂花钱。

这种模式直接说明了我们所说的人工智能的真正瓶颈，它不再是芯片，而是资本和同意。 甲骨文似乎正在测试它能在这两者上发挥多大作用。

新的削减落在残酷的一年之上。 在截至 2026 年 5 月 31 日的财年中，甲骨文裁员约 21,000 个，降幅约 13%，员工人数从约 162,000 人减少至约 141,000 人。

该公司在此期间记入了 18 亿美元的重组费用，在会计完成前预计将高达 21 亿美元。

造成这次裁员的原因是甲骨文提出的裁员理由。 在其自己的文件中，该公司将减少部分归因于“人工智能技术的采用和部署”。

换句话说，作为增长引擎出售的相同技术也是让数千人回家的理由。

跟着钱走，逻辑就会变得更清晰，甚至更舒服。 甲骨文竞相建设数据中心以支撑其云计算雄心，其资本支出在 2026 财年达到约 557 亿美元，高于一年前的 212 亿美元。 对于甲骨文这样规模的公司来说，一年内投入的资金是一笔非凡的资金。

支付这笔费用意味着深入债务市场。 甲骨文的运营现金缺口约为 237 亿美元，一年内筹集了约 430 亿美元的债务，预计还会筹集 400 亿美元左右，并通过股本补充 50 亿美元。

简而言之，扩建的资金是借来的，而不是自掏腰包，这种结构会让公司面临风险，如果它所押注的人工智能需求到达的速度比承诺的要慢。

基础业务几乎没有停滞不前。 随着对人工智能计算能力的需求不断攀升，收入增长了 17%，而与亚马逊和微软相对应的 Oracle 云基础设施增长了 77%。 从表面上看，这家公司在这场花费巨资参加的竞赛中获胜。

不过，投资者并不相信。 今年迄今为止，甲骨文股价已下跌约 26%，这是对以稳定盈利能力为赌注未来人工智能需求的战略的严厉判决。

市场似乎在询问回报是否足以证明借贷的合理性，但目前它对此不以为然。 股价下跌一个季度并不是相信这个故事的市场的反应。

去掉行话，算术就很明显了。 甲骨文正在削减人力成本来为机器提供资金，为此承担了大量债务，并在等待赌注获得回报的同时看着自己的估值下滑。 这是目前整个行业普遍面临的人工智能资本支出紧缩的清晰例证。

甲骨文并不是唯一一家进行这种交易的公司。 在整个行业中，企业一直在将工资转化为人工智能资本支出，将工资视为一种成本，重新分配给芯片和服务器大厅。 甲骨文的不同寻常之处在于，这些数字赤裸裸地揭示了这一选择。

对于本月面临削减的数千人来说，宏观经济框架提供了冰冷的安慰。 这些都是真实的工作，在真实的团队中，在日历和资产负债表规定的最后期限前被取消。

对人工智能的赌博最终是否会证明甲骨文的支出是正确的，现在为此付费的人们将无法得知。
